prize_parts.citation: For the theoretical prediction of the quantum spin Hall effect and topological insulators and its first experimental observation, establishing band topology as an organizing principle of quantum matter.

statement.case_for: Topological insulators introduced a new organizing principle for electronic matter, the Z2 invariant and protected boundary states, and the idea is concrete, original and testable. It was followed by a decisive experiment (HgTe quantum wells) and by two decades of independent confirmation in many material families and with transport and spectroscopic probes. The influence on condensed matter, spintronics, superconductivity and topological quantum computation proposals is broad, and the field is mature rather than still forming. As a statistical physicist I also value that the central object, a topological invariant of the band structure that survives disorder, is a robust statement and not a model-dependent claim. After reading colleagues' opening ballots I move my preferred trio from Kane, Molenkamp and Hasan to Kane, Mele and Molenkamp, because the quantum spin Hall prediction and the first observation of it form the cleanest theory-plus-experiment chain in the candidate.
statement.case_against: The credit story is incomplete whatever three names we choose. The Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang HgTe proposal, which made Molenkamp's experiment possible, is not representable among the credited names, and Shoucheng Zhang's death means it cannot be repaired by time. Three-dimensional topological insulators (Fu-Kane-Mele; Hasan) and the quantum anomalous Hall effect (Xue) are distinct strands that a Kane-Mele-Molenkamp prize leaves out. The 2016 prize on topological phases also covers related territory, and applications remain mostly prospective, so a sceptic can say the prize would be on time for the science but incomplete in attribution.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks B045 first with Kane, Mele and Molenkamp, as a compact theory-plus-experiment prize, while admitting that the omitted HgTe theorists and the 3D strand complicate allocation.
responses.response: I now agree with the trio, and I am changing my own opening choice of Hasan for Mele. Mele is a co-author of the Z2 theory of the quantum spin Hall state, and leaving him out in favour of an experimental ARPES strand would misrepresent who made the prediction. I do not agree that the missing Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal is a minor footnote. It is the reason Molenkamp's experiment was done in HgTe at all, and the citation should be worded around the quantum spin Hall effect and its first observation, so that it does not overclaim.

responses.point: Johansson ranks B004 first with Kane, Molenkamp and Xue (a Kane-Molenkamp pairing in his own proposal), and treats the quantum anomalous Hall effect as a distinct later step while noting that B045 overlaps.
responses.response: I agree that the topological-insulator case is the strongest in the shortlist, but I disagree that the quantum anomalous Hall effect belongs in the same citation. Xue's result depends on magnetic doping and on a lower-temperature regime, and it is a realisation of a different effect, so it mixes two achievements into one three-name string and leaves Mele out. Your two-name Kane-Molenkamp version is cleaner than the three-name B004, but it drops Mele, whose contribution to the theory is as central as Kane's. I would keep B004 as an alternative only if the committee decided that Mele cannot be credited.

responses.point: Pearce ranks the optical lattice clocks first and baryon acoustic oscillations second, with B045 third (Kane, Mele, Molenkamp), judging the clocks a clean, mature two-person case.
responses.response: I accept that the clock case is clean in its attribution, which is better than for B045, and I rank it as my first alternative. My reservation is the category: the lattice clock is a very large advance in what can be measured, but its main output so far is a better instrument and tests of constants at ever smaller uncertainties, not a new class of phenomena. Topological band theory changed how a whole field classifies matter. The Frequency-comb prize in 2005 and the 2012 prize on single-ion control also make the clock look more like a continuation of a recognised line than the topological case does. I would not call that a decisive argument against the clocks.

responses.point: Kroll puts optical lattice clocks first as an enabling instrument-level advance with stable interpretation, and places the Kane, Molenkamp and Xue topological-insulator candidate third because of mixed credit.
responses.response: Your point that instrument-level advances have repeatedly been recognised is fair, and clocks do have the advantage of a pending redefinition of the second. I disagree that the mixed credit in B004 should be solved by Xue, since that is the reason I prefer B045 to B004. The credit problem in topological insulators is that of which theorists to include, not that experiments are missing, and Kane-Mele-Molenkamp resolves most of it with a clear division between theory and experiment. I would be interested in whether you see the redefinition as a precondition for the clock prize, because if it is, the timing is less urgent than the opening ballots suggest.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks twisted bilayer graphene first as a rare theory-then-experiment case with a new field behind it, and puts the topological-insulator candidate third because the Kane-Mele versus Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang allocation is contested.
responses.response: I take the field-creating argument for B030 seriously and rank it as my second alternative. My reservation is maturity: the pairing mechanism and the nature of the correlated states are still debated, and sensitivity to twist-angle disorder is known, so the committee would be recognising a field whose basic interpretation is unsettled. For topological insulators the interpretation has been stable for over a decade. I agree with you that the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang allocation is the real weakness of B045, and I do not think it can be fully resolved; we can only word the citation so that it does not claim the HgTe proposal.

uncertainties: How the committee should treat the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang HgTe proposal and the late Shoucheng Zhang when none of them can be credited from the supplied names.
Whether Hasan's three-dimensional topological insulator work should be recognised in a separate part or left out; a one-prize configuration with Kane, Mele and Molenkamp cannot also include it.
How much weight the 2016 prize on topological phases should have against a second topology-related award.
Whether the optical lattice clock candidate would be strengthened or weakened by the timing of the redefinition of the second.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my provided profile. I have no documented personal or institutional connection to Kane, Mele, Molenkamp, Hasan or the other shortlisted candidates, and my own research in statistical physics, random matrices and neural networks is not in any shortlisted subject.
